title: MIN and MAX: Read Just the Ends
description: MIN/MAX over an unindexed column scans the table; an index lets the engine read a single value from one end.
narrative:
## Scenario
A dashboard shows the earliest and latest order dates:

```sql
SELECT MIN(OrderDate), MAX(OrderDate) FROM Orders;
```

It reads the **entire** 200,000-row table every time it refreshes.

## Why it's slow
Nothing indexes `OrderDate`. To find the smallest and largest values SQL Server has no choice but to look at **every row** — a **Clustered Index Scan** feeding an aggregate. Cost grows with the table.

## The concept
In an index, rows are stored **in order**, so the minimum sits at one end and the maximum at the other. With an index on `OrderDate`, SQL Server can satisfy `MIN` and `MAX` by reading just the **two ends** of the index (a pair of tiny `TOP`/seek operations) instead of scanning all rows.

## What to look for
- Before: a **Clustered Index Scan** reading ~all pages (hundreds+ logical reads).
- After: a plan with **`TOP`** operators and only a handful of logical reads.

The fix is a nonclustered index on `OrderDate`.
startingQuery: SELECT MIN(OrderDate) AS Earliest, MAX(OrderDate) AS Latest FROM Orders;
hints: MIN/MAX over an unindexed column must scan every row — look for a Clustered Index Scan in the plan.
In an ordered index the smallest value is at one end and the largest at the other; SQL can read just those.
Create the index: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate ON dbo.Orders(OrderDate);
